name: Honey (topical)

lead: Topical honey is used as a mask or skincare ingredient for hydration and a softer, brighter look. It is hygroscopic, so it attracts and holds water at the skin surface, and it has a long folk history on burns and wounds.

Its antibacterial properties are attributed to compounds such as methylglyoxal and hydrogen peroxide, under preliminary study. Trials exist for wounds, mouth ulcers and eye conditions, and medical-grade honey products are FDA-approved for minor wounds and burns; trials on cosmetic brightening were not found.

paras: People apply it as a thin layer for a short wash-off mask, mix it with ingredients such as oats or yoghurt, or use it as an ingredient in cleansers and creams. Hydration shows right after rinsing.
Generally well tolerated as a food. Infant botulism is the best-documented risk of honey, so it is not given to infants under one, and allergy is possible in sensitive people.

web.title: Honey as a moisturizing ingredient: systematic review

angle.text: Honey draws moisture into the skin surface, so it is used in masks and skincare for softer, hydrated, glowier-looking skin, and some people use it for brightening and blemishes. Its documented research is in wound care.

lead: Topical honey is honey applied to the skin, either as a home face mask and spot treatment or as a processed ingredient in commercial moisturisers, cleansers and masks. Honey is hygroscopic, meaning it draws in moisture, which is the basis for its use as a humectant that leaves skin feeling softer and more hydrated.[1] It has a long folk history on burns and skin injuries, and some medical-grade honey products are approved by the FDA for minor wounds and burns.[1]

In appearance skincare, honey is used for hydration, smoothness and a clearer-looking, brighter complexion, and mānuka honey from New Zealand is the best-known premium variety.[2] Clinical research on honey has concentrated on wound care and mucosal conditions, but a 2026 systematic review of cosmetic trials identified five controlled studies, three of which reported benefits for hydration, smoothness or healing; the authors called the evidence limited and inconsistent and asked for trials focused on cosmetic outcomes.[3]

Wikipedia's Honey article reports that evidence is moderate to low for uses beyond burns and post-operative wounds.[1] Honey is generally regarded as safe on skin in everyday amounts, with infant botulism the best-known risk of honey as a food.[1]
infobox: Hygroscopic (humectant); acidic, with glucose oxidase generating hydrogen peroxide[1]
Mānuka honey (Leptospermum scoparium), graded by MGO or UMF[2]
Masks, cleansers, moisturisers, lip and hand products
Not recommended for infants under one (botulism)[1]

paras: Honey appears in DIY face masks and in commercial moisturisers, cleansers and masks, usually for hydration and softening. Its sugars attract and hold water at the skin surface, and its mild acidity (average pH about 3.9) and enzyme-generated hydrogen peroxide are cited by proponents as reasons for its use on blemish-prone skin.[1] Traditional-brightener claims are common in beauty writing; controlled data on skin tone or pigmentation have not been published.

In the cosmetic trials reviewed in 2026, honey was tested in creams at concentrations of 5 to 15% and in glycerinated honey extracts, and outcomes included skin hydration, smoothness and wrinkle measures.[3]

Honey has long been used as a topical antibacterial in traditional medicine; Greek, Egyptian, Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine used it on wounds and burns, and its antibacterial effects were first demonstrated in 1892 by Bernardus van Ketel.[1] Wikipedia describes preliminary evidence that honey heals partial-thickness burns four to five days faster than other dressings and moderate evidence for faster healing of post-operative infections, with low-quality evidence for other wounds.[1] Clinical reviews list honey among topical options for MRSA and chronic wounds.[4][5]

Honey is mainly fructose and glucose, a supersaturated sugar solution of roughly 15.5 to 18% water. Bees add glucose oxidase, which produces gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide, and honey has broad-spectrum activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, though potency varies widely between honeys.[1] Methylglyoxal, hydrogen peroxide and the peptide royalisin are under study as antimicrobial components.[1]
Honey absorbs moisture from the air depending on humidity, which is why it is stored sealed and why it behaves as a humectant in creams.[1]

Mānuka honey is made by honey bees from the nectar of the mānuka tree, native to New Zealand and coastal Australia, and is the variety most often used in wound dressings and premium skincare.[2] Wikipedia credits methylglyoxal (MGO) with much of its distinctive activity; New Zealand honey is graded by MGO content (mg/kg) and by the Unique Mānuka Factor (UMF), for example 263 mg/kg MGO corresponding to UMF 10 and 829 mg/kg to UMF 20.[2] Compounds such as leptosperin are described as unique to mānuka honey.[2]

New Zealand introduced a five-attribute science definition (four chemical markers and one DNA marker) effective January 2018, and Australia has its own standard.[2] The UMF Honey Association has reported that around six times as much honey is sold as mānuka as New Zealand produces, and competing grading labels and adulterated products have been reported.[2] Between 2022 and 2025 the FDA sent warning letters to manufacturers of mānuka products marketed as eye treatments or allergy remedies, which the agency said were unapproved drugs with unsupported health claims.[2]

Cosmetic skin outcomes: a 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology identified five controlled clinical studies of honey as a moisturizing ingredient. A Polish hand-cream study with multifloral honey at 5, 10 and 15% reported, after four weeks, hydration gains up to 29.7%, smoothness up to 21.3% and reduced wrinkle area up to 21.4%, with the 5% cream performing best. A Czech study of forearm emulsions reported that a glycerinated honey extract improved moisturizing and barrier properties. Studies of post-cesarean scars and of mānuka honey after tattooing found no significant difference from placebo or standard cream, and a study of honey dressings on pressure injuries in critically ill children found faster healing (7 versus 9 days). No adverse effects were reported. The authors noted only five trials with differing honeys and designs, no meta-analysis, and called for further cosmetic-focused trials.[3]

Wound care: a 2024 meta-analysis of eight studies with 906 participants found honey dressings shortened chronic wound healing time and raised the percentage healed, without significant differences in healing rate or bacterial clearance time, and noted possible painful discomfort during treatment.[6] A 2023 meta-analysis reported faster recovery, less pain and quicker granulation with honey in diabetic foot ulcers.[7]

Other settings: a randomized, blinded trial compared honey with a topical corticosteroid for recurrent minor aphthous ulcers.[8] A randomized assessor-masked trial of 16% mānuka honey eye-drops studied meibomian gland dysfunction in 59 patients.[9] Registered trials include honey dressings versus EUSOL for wound infection (n=326), honey in deep neck abscess care, mānuka honey after third-molar surgery, diabetic foot ulcers, perineal tear healing and honey versus alcohol as a skin disinfectant.[10][11][12][13][14]

Honey is generally considered safe in typical food amounts, but infants under one year can develop botulism from honey containing Clostridium botulinum spores.[1] Wikipedia also notes possible interactions with allergies and that people with weakened immune systems may face infection risk; some honeys are toxic, such as 'mad honey' containing grayanotoxins and certain New Zealand honeys containing tutin.[1] Topical allergic reactions in sensitive individuals are possible. No adverse effects were reported in the five cosmetic trials, though the review described the sample sizes as small.[3]

Honey is often combined in DIY masks with ingredients such as oats, yogurt or cinnamon, and appears alongside propolis, royal jelly and beeswax in bee-product skincare.[3] Other humectants used in commercial moisturisers include glycerin and hyaluronic acid; the 2020 Czech study tested glycerin-based honey extracts.[3]

lore.intro: In home-skincare and beauty discussion, honey is described as a pantry-staple mask ingredient for hydration, glow and blemishes, with mānuka honey as the premium option.[2][3]
